faq.q: Why is the empty‑can test specific for supraspinatus?

faq.a: No; early infection may show only soft‑tissue swelling, so aspiration is essential if clinical suspicion is high.
faq.q: Can a normal X‑ray rule out septic arthritis?

faq.a: Assess for pain, then test for rotator‑cuff weakness; if pain dominates, consider impingement or effusion before imaging.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with painful shoulder swelling and fever—what is your next diagnostic step? — Perform joint aspiration; it confirms infection and guides antibiotics.
How does the Neer sign differentiate impingement from adhesive capsulitis? — Impingement causes pain on forced elevation; capsulitis limits active and passive motion without pain on impingement.
A patient cannot externally rotate the shoulder; which nerve is most likely injured? — Axillary nerve injury; it supplies teres minor and contributes to external rotation.
In a resource‑limited setting, how would you confirm a rotator‑cuff tear without MRI? — Use bedside ultrasound or clinical empty‑can test combined with pain‑limited active ROM.
What red‑flag features in shoulder pain demand urgent referral? — Fever, rapidly expanding swelling, neurovascular loss, or suspicion of TB/osteomyelitis.
Why is the apprehension test important before reduction of a dislocated shoulder? — It identifies persistent instability that may need surgical stabilization.
A patient with HIV presents with chronic shoulder pain and a draining sinus—what is the most likely diagnosis? — TB osteomyelitis of the proximal humerus; treat with anti‑TB regimen.
What management steps follow a confirmed septic shoulder arthritis? — Urgent drainage, appropriate antibiotics, and immobilisation; monitor for osteomyelitis.
ai.title: Shoulder Examination
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: A systematic shoulder exam links anatomy to common pathologies seen in low‑resource settings. It guides the student to assess structures, recognise red‑flags, and plan investigations without relying on advanced tests.

b: Four main components: glenohumeral joint, acromioclavicular (AC) joint, scapulothoracic articulation, and surrounding muscles/tendons.
Common local conditions in East Africa: rotator‑cuff tendinopathy, septic arthritis, TB osteomyelitis, trauma from falls or road traffic accidents.
sections.p: The shoulder is a mobile ball‑and‑socket joint that balances wide range of motion with stability. Examination must identify pain generators, functional loss and signs of infection or trauma.

The glenoid fossa of the scapula articulates with the humeral head. The rotator‑cuff (Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis) caps the joint, while the deltoid and trapezius provide gross movement.

b: Infection can spread from the skin or from haematogenous sources (e.g., malaria‑related bacteremia).
sections.p: Anteriorly the joint is adjacent to the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus; posteriorly it lies against the scapular spine. The subacromial bursa lies between the rotator‑cuff and acromion.

b: Ischemia of the supraspinatus tendon predisposes to tears.
sections.p: The anterior and posterior humeral circumflex arteries, branches of the axillary artery, perfuse the joint capsule and rotator‑cuff tendons.

b: Axillary nerve injury causes deltoid weakness and loss of shoulder abduction beyond 15°.
sections.p: The suprascapular nerve (C5‑C6) innervates supraspinatus and infraspinatus; the axillary nerve (C5‑C6) supplies deltoid and teres minor; the subscapular nerves supply subscapularis.

b: Loss of external rotation often points to infraspinatus pathology.
sections.p: Provides elevation, rotation and scapulothoracic rhythm for overhead activities. Stability is achieved by static (labrum, capsule) and dynamic (rotator‑cuff) structures.

b: Dislocation: loss of the rounded contour, palpable humeral head inferior to the glenoid.
Septic arthritis: fever, warm swollen joint, limited active/passive motion; common organisms include Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
TB osteomyelitis: chronic pain, swelling, sinus formation; may mimic chronic rotator‑cuff disease.
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, the most encountered problems are traumatic dislocation, rotator‑cuff tear, septic arthritis, and TB osteomyelitis of the proximal humerus.

t.b: Detects fractures, dislocation, joint space narrowing; if unavailable, use clinical displacement signs.
Answers whether effusion is inflammatory/infectious; Gram stain and Ziehl‑Neelsen if TB suspected.
Identifies rotator‑cuff tears and effusions; portable units are useful where X‑ray is limited.

b: Inspection: look for asymmetry, bruising, muscle wasting.
Palpation: tip of acromion, coracoid, greater tuberosity, AC joint.
Active ROM: forward flexion, abduction, external rotation; note pain limits.
Passive ROM: compare side‑to‑side; pain suggests intra‑articular pathology.
Strength: 5‑point scale; test supraspinatus (empty‑can), infraspinatus (external rotation), subscapularis (internal rotation).
sections.p: Perform the exam with the patient supine or sitting, progressing from inspection to palpation, range of motion, strength testing and special tests.

t.b: Is pain reproduced with resisted forward elevation in internal rotation? Positive = supraspinatus tendinopathy/tear.
Pain on passive forward elevation with scapular stabilization? Positive = subacromial impingement.
Pain/guarding when the arm is abducted and externally rotated? Positive = anterior instability/dislocation risk.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever with rapidly enlarging shoulder swelling
Severe shoulder pain after trauma with neurovascular deficit
Unexplained weight loss and chronic shoulder sinus suggesting TB
